r: RA 9522 (baselines law) is constitutional. UNCLOS III and baselines laws do not add to or reduce territory; States acquire or lose territory only by occupation, accretion, cession and prescription. Treating the Kalayaan Island Group and Scarborough Shoal as a ‘regime of islands’ does not cede them. RA 9522 is only a statutory tool to demarcate the maritime zones and continental shelf under UNCLOS. Calling the waters inside the baselines ‘archipelagic waters’ subject to innocent passage and sea lanes passage does not violate Art. I: the Philippines keeps sovereignty over them, and those passage rights already bind it under international law.
f: Law professors and students, as citizens and taxpayers, challenged the 2009 baselines law for allegedly shrinking territory and converting internal waters into archipelagic waters.
h: Petition dismissed; RA 9522 upheld.
x: West Philippine Sea stories: distinguish territory (sovereignty) from maritime zones (sovereign rights under UNCLOS). Also applies to the Maritime Zones Act (RA 12064, 2024) and the Archipelagic Sea Lanes Act (RA 12065, 2024).
s: Baselines law valid: UNCLOS neither adds to nor reduces territory; KIG and Scarborough as regimes of islands.

n: The South China Sea Arbitration (Philippines v. China)
r: China’s claim to historic rights within the nine-dash line has no legal basis to the extent it exceeds UNCLOS entitlements. No Spratly feature is a fully entitled island that generates an EEZ. China violated the Philippines’ sovereign rights in its EEZ. Whatever historic rights China had were extinguished by UNCLOS to the extent incompatible with it. A feature’s entitlement is judged in its natural condition: one that cannot sustain human habitation or economic life of its own is a rock with only a 12-nautical-mile territorial sea, and artificial islands or outside supplies do not change that.
f: The Philippines brought an UNCLOS Annex VII arbitration over China’s nine-dash line, the status of features, and Chinese conduct (fishing, reclamation, obstruction).
h: Award in favor of the Philippines on most claims (July 12, 2016). The tribunal did not rule on sovereignty over features. China was also found to have interfered with Philippine fishing and petroleum exploration, to have harmed the marine environment through reclamation at seven Spratly features, to have prevented traditional fishing at Scarborough Shoal, and to have created a serious risk of collision there in 2012.
x: Use for any West Philippine Sea fact pattern: maritime entitlements, EEZ rights, enforcement. Remember the award decides entitlements, not sovereignty.
s: Nine-dash line has no legal basis beyond UNCLOS; no Spratly feature generates an EEZ.

n: Province of North Cotabato v. GRP Peace Panel on Ancestral Domain
r: The MOA-AD was unconstitutional: the Executive cannot guarantee constitutional amendments or create a ‘Bangsamoro Juridical Entity’ with associative status, which presupposes a State. The case was decided despite mootness (the MOA-AD was not signed) because of grave constitutional issues. The President’s power to negotiate peace is implied from her powers as Chief Executive and Commander-in-Chief, and she may submit the solutions she favors to Congress as recommendations; what she cannot do is implement them unilaterally or guarantee to a third party that the amendments will be adopted. The panel also committed grave abuse by not consulting the affected LGUs and indigenous peoples (right to information; LGC; IPRA).
f: The GRP panel initialed a Memorandum of Agreement on Ancestral Domain with the MILF, promising to effect the constitutional and legal changes needed; a TRO stopped the signing.
h: MOA-AD declared contrary to law and the Constitution.
x: Peace agreement stories: the President may negotiate and propose but cannot bind Congress or the people to amend the Constitution. Contrast PHILCONSA (2016) on ripeness.
s: MOA-AD void: the Executive cannot guarantee amendments or create an associative juridical entity.

n: Cruz v. Secretary of Environment and Natural Resources
r: The constitutionality of IPRA (RA 8371) was challenged under the Regalian Doctrine. The Court was split 7–7; after redeliberation the tie remained, so the petition was dismissed and the law stands (Rule 56 on ties). Under Rule 56, Sec. 7 of the Rules of Court, a tie in an original action that persists after redeliberation means dismissal: IPRA stands, but no ruling on its validity is made. Justice Puno’s separate opinion (native title under Cariño as an exception to the Regalian Doctrine) is the usual cite for upholding IPRA.
f: Citizens and taxpayers attacked IPRA’s recognition of ancestral domains, including natural resources, as ‘private but community property’ of indigenous peoples.
h: Petition dismissed on a tie vote; IPRA not declared unconstitutional.
x: Use for the effect of a tie vote and for native title versus the Regalian Doctrine (Puno’s separate opinion). Also listed under Judiciary (Voting).
s: IPRA survives a 7–7 tie: the petition is dismissed, so the law stands without a ruling on its validity.

r: A natural-born Filipino who reacquires citizenship under RA 9225 and runs for office must (1) take the oath of allegiance and (2) execute a personal, sworn renunciation of foreign citizenship before filing the COC. Winning the election does not cure ineligibility.
f: A naturalized US citizen reacquired Philippine citizenship, ran for Manila councilor, and won, but never executed a sworn renunciation.
h: Disqualified; COMELEC’s annulment of her proclamation was affirmed and the next-ranked qualified candidate proclaimed.
x: Dual citizen candidates. Note: the remedy of proclaiming the next-ranked candidate (the second-placer rule) was abandoned in Mangudadatu v. COMELEC (2025).

r: An illegitimate child of a Filipino father and an alien mother is a Filipino citizen if paternity is proven; the 1935 Constitution’s ‘father is a citizen’ rule draws no distinction by legitimacy. Evidence suggested FPJ’s grandfather became a Filipino under the Philippine Bill of 1902. Civil-law rules on legitimacy govern private rights such as support and succession, not citizenship, which is a matter of political law. Lorenzo Pou, a Spanish subject presumed to have resided in the Philippines and who died in Pangasinan in 1954, became Filipino by the Philippine Bill of 1902, and that citizenship passed to Allan Poe and then to FPJ, whose filiation was shown by his birth certificate.
f: Petitions to disqualify Fernando Poe Jr. for President argued he was illegitimate and so followed his American mother’s citizenship.
h: Petitions dismissed; COMELEC did not commit grave abuse in refusing to cancel the COC. Jurisdiction over a President’s qualifications after the election belongs to the PET.
x: Use for natural-born status by blood (jus sanguinis), the 1935 rules, and forum (COMELEC before the election; PET after).
s: An illegitimate child of a Filipino father is Filipino if paternity is proven (1935 Constitution).

r: Foundlings are natural-born citizens: the Constitution, its deliberations, the statistical probability that a child found in the Philippines has Filipino parents, and international law support a presumption of Filipino parentage. Grace Poe was qualified as Senator. The international-law basis is the generally accepted principle (1930 Hague Convention, Art. 14; 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness, Art. 2) that a foundling is presumed born in, and of nationals of, the State where found; the Philippines is bound through Art. II, Sec. 2 even without ratifying those treaties. Poe’s reacquisition under RA 9225 restored, rather than replaced, her natural-born status.
f: A defeated senatorial candidate filed quo warranto in the SET, arguing Senator Poe, a foundling, was not natural-born.
h: The SET did not commit grave abuse; petition dismissed.
x: Foundling status and the SET’s jurisdiction over a sitting Senator’s qualifications. RA 11767 (Foundling Recognition and Protection Act, 2022) now presumes foundlings found in the Philippines natural-born.
g: Gatmaytan, ‘Hard Cases Make Bad Movies: The Candidates Poe and Philippine Citizenship Law as Screenplay’ (2021) is assigned with this case. The Poe cases appeared on his 2015 midterm (forum, ripeness, and whether the SET and the PET may reach different results).
s: Foundlings are presumed natural-born; Poe qualified as Senator.

r: Election of Philippine citizenship (for those born of Filipino mothers before Jan. 17, 1973) may be implied from positive acts such as voting and holding office. A person whose father was naturalized while he was a minor, and who elected, is natural-born. Residence means domicile and is not lost by temporary absence. The sworn statement is for those who still have to elect; for those already treated as Filipinos when the time to elect came, deliberate acts such as entering a profession open only to Filipinos, holding an office requiring citizenship, and voting are election enough. Art. IV, Sec. 1(3) and the ‘deemed natural-born’ clause correct the 1935 rule that only the father’s citizenship passed, and apply to those who elected before 1987.
f: Jose Ong Jr., born in Samar to a Chinese father later naturalized and a Filipina mother, was elected to Congress; losing candidates said he was not natural-born or a resident.
h: HRET ruling upheld; Ong was natural-born and a resident. The Court reviews the HRET only for grave abuse.
x: Election of citizenship; who is natural-born under Art. IV, Sec. 2; and HRET deference.
s: Election of citizenship may be implied from positive acts like voting; residence means domicile.

r: A naturalized Filipino who later obtains and uses a foreign passport and declares a foreign nationality in documents expressly renounces Philippine citizenship. Citizenship is not a commodity to be displayed when required and suppressed when convenient. A renunciation is express when it is made known distinctly and explicitly; Yu’s acts, taken together, met that standard.
f: A naturalized Filipino of Portuguese origin renewed and used a Portuguese passport and described himself as Portuguese in business papers.
h: He was held to have lost Philippine citizenship; his detention for deportation was valid.
x: Loss of citizenship by express renunciation through conduct.

r: Repatriation under RA 8171 is done by filing with the Special Committee on Naturalization, not the regional trial court. An RTC that grants repatriation acts without jurisdiction. RA 965 and RA 2630 did not apply because they cover only those who lost citizenship by serving in, or taking a commission from, the armed forces of an allied country or the United States. RA 8171 covers Filipino women who lost citizenship by marrying aliens and natural-born Filipinos who lost it through political or economic necessity; repatriation is completed by taking the oath and registering it with the civil registry and the Bureau of Immigration.
f: A natural-born Filipino who became a US citizen petitioned the RTC to regain citizenship and took his oath there.
h: RTC proceedings void for lack of jurisdiction.
x: Right forum and mode for reacquiring citizenship.

r: Repatriation restores a person to his original status: a natural-born Filipino who lost citizenship (here by serving in the US armed forces) and is repatriated is again natural-born and may sit in the House. Citizenship is reacquired by naturalization, repatriation, or direct act of Congress. Repatriation needs only an oath of allegiance registered with the civil registry, not naturalization proceedings, so it recovers the original status. The Constitution recognizes only two kinds of citizens, natural-born and naturalized, and one who is not naturalized is natural-born.
f: Teodoro Cruz, a natural-born Filipino, became a US citizen through military service, was repatriated under RA 2630, and was elected Representative.
h: Cruz was natural-born and qualified; HRET upheld.
x: Use when a former Filipino who reacquired citizenship runs for an office requiring natural-born status (compare RA 9225 reacquisition, which also restores natural-born status).
s: Repatriation restores natural-born status.

n: Tan Co v. Civil Register of Manila
r: CA 473 (minor children of a naturalized father become citizens) and the law under which the father was naturalized (LOI 270) are in pari materia: minor children of those naturalized under LOI 270 also become Filipinos. Under CA 473, Sec. 15, minor children born in the Philippines of a person naturalized become citizens. LOI 270 and CA 473 share the same purpose (to naturalize aliens who have shown loyalty and affinity to the country), so they are read together as one law.
f: Siblings sought to correct their birth records to show Philippine citizenship after their father was naturalized under LOI 270 while they were minors.
h: RTC dismissal set aside; the petition for correction of the birth records (a substantial change, allowed in an adversarial Rule 108 proceeding) was ordered reinstated and heard, since Sec. 15 of CA 473 extends to minor children of those naturalized under LOI 270.
x: Derivative naturalization of minor children.

r: Election under CA 625 requires a sworn statement of election, an oath of allegiance, and registration with the civil registry, within a reasonable time (generally three years) after majority. Election cannot be done by judicial declaration. The three-year ‘reasonable time’ may be extended only in special circumstances, which Sagun did not show.
f: A legitimate child of a Chinese father and Filipina mother took an oath 12 years after majority and never registered it, then sought a court declaration.
h: Petition dismissed; no valid election, and courts cannot declare citizenship in a petition of this kind.
x: Contrast Co v. HRET: implied election applies only to those already treated as Filipino; Sagun’s formal election was late and defective.

r: Naturalization is a privilege, strictly construed. Character witnesses must be credible persons with personal knowledge vouching for the applicant; omissions in required petition contents (e.g., former residences) are fatal. CA 473 requires two credible witnesses, persons of good standing who can vouch for the applicant from intimate knowledge, and the statement of former residences is jurisdictional.
f: A Manila-born son of Chinese parents applied for judicial naturalization under CA 473.
h: Petition denied.
x: Judicial naturalization requirements.

r: Failure to attach a certificate of arrival to a petition for naturalization is fatal; it is separate from the declaration of intention and is not excused by exemption from the latter. The certificate of arrival shows that the applicant is a documented alien whose entry and stay were lawful and in good faith; its absence makes the petition incomplete and it must be denied outright.
f: An applicant exempt from filing a declaration of intention did not attach his certificate of arrival.
h: Petition denied.
x: Strict compliance in naturalization.

r: A ‘lucrative trade, profession or lawful occupation’ means income with an appreciable margin over expenses, proven by documents; a comfortable lifestyle is not proof. An income tax return showing income enough for basic needs does not prove the appreciable margin.
f: An Indian national applied for naturalization but did not show his actual financial status.
h: Petition denied.
x: Strict proof of naturalization qualifications.

r: Using a foreign passport after renouncing foreign citizenship recants the renunciation; the candidate becomes a dual citizen again and is disqualified (LGC Sec. 40(d)). Where the COC is void from the start, votes for the ineligible candidate are stray.
f: Rommel Arnado reacquired citizenship and renounced US citizenship, then twice used his US passport, and won as mayor.
h: Arnado disqualified; the next-ranked qualified candidate (Maquiling) was ordered proclaimed.
x: Dual citizen candidate who keeps acting as a foreigner. Remedy update: the second-placer rule was abandoned in Mangudadatu (2025); the vacancy is now filled by succession.
s: Using a foreign passport after renouncing recants the renunciation: disqualified.

r: Citizenship for a local elective official is required at the latest at proclamation or the start of the term. Repatriation under PD 725 is curative and retroacts to the date of application. A second-placer cannot be proclaimed when the winner is disqualified (except when voters knowingly threw away their votes).
f: Frivaldo, a naturalized US citizen, won as Sorsogon governor; his repatriation oath was taken on the day his term began.
h: Frivaldo was qualified; the second-placer (Lee) was not entitled to the seat.
x: Timing of the citizenship qualification for local officials; retroactive repatriation.
w: The masterfile digest’s top ‘Doctrine’ line states the opposite (that the second-placer must be declared winner). Its own Holdings section says Frivaldo won and the second-placer cannot be proclaimed. Rely on the Holdings.
s: Citizenship of a local official is required at proclamation or start of term; repatriation retroacts.

r: RA 9225 requires a personal and sworn renunciation before an officer authorized to administer oaths; an unsworn renunciation filed abroad does not comply. Foreign law must be proved; it is not judicially noticed.
f: A repatriated former Australian citizen renounced Australian citizenship by an unsworn declaration and won as vice-mayor.
h: Disqualified.
x: Strict form of the renunciation; proof of foreign law.

r: RA 9225 does not violate Art. IV, Sec. 5. Dual citizenship is not dual allegiance; the law concerns only Philippine citizenship and leaves foreign citizenship to foreign law. What dual allegiance is, and how to deal with it, is for Congress to define.
f: A petition for prohibition argued that letting reacquiring Filipinos keep foreign citizenship sanctions dual allegiance.
h: RA 9225 upheld.
x: Use against claims that dual citizens are ‘unconstitutional’ or that a body like the CSC may bar them without a law.
g: Gatmaytan’s book quotes the point that the Court cannot set the parameters of dual allegiance because the Constitution left that to Congress.

r: The RA 9225 oath-and-renunciation requirements apply only to dual citizens by naturalization who reacquire Philippine citizenship. A dual citizen by birth (Filipino father, American mother) need not renounce; filing a COC is itself an implied renunciation.
f: A Makati-born candidate for councilor with a Filipino father and American mother was disqualified by COMELEC for not renouncing US citizenship (based on a Consular Report of Birth Abroad).
h: COMELEC reversed; she was qualified. The consular report only recognized, not conferred, US citizenship.
x: Distinguish dual citizens by birth (no RA 9225 steps; Mercado v. Manzano rule) from those who reacquired citizenship (two-step RA 9225).
s: RA 9225 renunciation applies only to naturalized dual citizens who reacquire; dual citizens by birth need not renounce.

r: Loss of Philippine citizenship is not presumed. A person born of a Filipino father is presumed to remain Filipino until loss under CA 63 is proved (naturalization abroad, express renunciation, oath of allegiance to another State, and the other statutory grounds). Holding an alien certificate of registration (ACR), or being certified as an American, is not express renunciation; at most it shows dual citizenship, which by itself does not cost Philippine citizenship.
f: Emilio ‘Lito’ Osmeña ran for Governor of Cebu in the January 1988 local elections. Jose Aznar sought his disqualification as an alien, citing an ACR and permit to reside issued to him as an American and certifications that he was a US citizen. Osmeña showed that he was the son of a Filipino father, held a Philippine passport, had lived continuously in the Philippines, and had been a registered voter since 1965. He won and was proclaimed; COMELEC dismissed the petition.
h: Petition dismissed; COMELEC’s ruling for Osmeña affirmed. There was no proof that he had been naturalized abroad or had expressly renounced Philippine citizenship, so he remained a Filipino and qualified.
x: Candidate attacked as a foreigner on the strength of alien registration or foreign documents: the challenger must prove a CA 63 ground of loss. Contrast Frivaldo (1989) and Labo (1989), where naturalization abroad was proved, and Willie Yu, where conduct amounted to express renunciation. Mercado v. Manzano (1999) later built on Aznar in separating dual citizenship from dual allegiance.
test: Has the citizen lost Philippine citizenship? (1) Start from the presumption of continuing citizenship (born of a Filipino parent). (2) The challenger must prove a CA 63 ground, such as naturalization abroad, express renunciation, or an oath to another State. (3) An ACR, foreign residence documents, or being ‘considered’ a foreigner by another State is not enough; it shows at most dual citizenship.
s: An ACR does not mean renunciation: loss of citizenship must be proved, and dual citizenship alone does not disqualify.

r: For election purposes, residence means domicile. Domicile is not lost by working and even voting elsewhere unless three things concur: physical presence in the new place, intention to remain there, and intention to abandon the old domicile.
f: Pedro Gallego, a native of Abuyog, Leyte, lost the 1937 mayoral race and in 1938 took work as a nurseryman at a Bureau of Forestry plantation in Malaybalay, Bukidnon, where he obtained a residence certificate and registered and voted. He won the December 1940 Abuyog mayoral race by about 800 votes; the loser, Vera, challenged his residence, and the CFI and Court of Appeals declared his election void.
h: Reversed: he had not lost his Abuyog domicile and was qualified. His stay in Malaybalay was for employment, not to settle there indefinitely.
x: Residence or domicile questions for voters and candidates.
test: New domicile by choice: (1) bodily presence in the new place; (2) animus manendi (intent to remain); (3) animus non revertendi (intent to abandon the old).

r: A change of domicile must be voluntary. Leaving the country out of fear for one’s safety after EDSA is not abandonment of domicile. Domicile is a fixed residence to which, when absent for some cause, one intends to return (animus revertendi). It is lost only by acquiring a domicile of choice, which needs bodily presence, intent to remain, and intent to abandon the old domicile.
f: Philip Romualdez fled to the US in 1986, returned in 1991, and registered in his old barangay in Leyte; his exclusion from the voters’ list was sought.
h: He remained a resident and a qualified voter.
x: Involuntary absence does not change domicile.
test: New domicile by choice: (1) bodily presence in the new place; (2) animus manendi (intent to remain); (3) animus non revertendi (intent to abandon the old). The change must also be voluntary.

r: Registration is a valid procedural regulation of suffrage, not a substantive requirement. COMELEC cannot be compelled to hold special registration within the 120-day prohibitive period of RA 8189, Sec. 8, and its ‘stand-by’ power may be used only if pre-election acts cannot reasonably be held within the law’s periods. Suffrage is not absolute: it is subject to substantive requirements (Art. V, Sec. 1) and procedural ones, chiefly registration, which the State may regulate under police power. The Court accepted COMELEC’s showing that the remaining pre-election work (project of precincts, boards of election inspectors, sealing the book of voters, printing the computerized voters’ list) left no time for special registration.
f: Youth groups sought a two-day special registration in February 2001, within 120 days of the May 2001 election.
h: Petitions dismissed.
x: Registration deadlines that fall within the statutory prohibitive period. Contrast Palatino.

r: Biometrics validation (RA 10367) is part of registration, a procedural regulation, not a ‘qualification’ or a prohibited ‘substantive requirement’ under Art. V, Sec. 1. It also passes strict scrutiny: a compelling interest in a clean voters’ list, pursued by the least restrictive means (deactivated voters may reactivate).
f: ‘No Bio, No Boto’: COMELEC would deactivate about 2.4 to 3 million voters without biometrics before the 2016 elections.
h: RA 10367 and the COMELEC resolutions upheld; the earlier TRO was lifted.
x: The 2015 Finals asked exactly this. Any new condition on voting: is it a qualification (only the Constitution and laws within Art. V may impose) or a registration procedure (valid if reasonable)?
s: Biometrics validation is a registration procedure, not a substantive requirement; passes strict scrutiny.

r: COMELEC cannot cut short the continuing registration Congress fixed in RA 8189, Sec. 8 (registration closes only 120 days before a regular election). Its stand-by power to fix other dates applies only when pre-election acts cannot reasonably be held within the statutory period, which COMELEC must show. Congress itself judged the 120-day and 90-day periods enough for COMELEC to prepare, and that legislative judgment binds COMELEC.
f: For the 2010 elections, COMELEC moved the registration deadline to October 31, 2009, months before the 120-day prohibitive period.
h: Petition granted; the resolution setting the October 31 deadline was declared void and registration extended until January 9, 2010.
x: Distinguish AKBAYAN: there the extension sought fell inside the prohibitive period; here it did not. The 2015 Finals (Ridon, October 31, 2015 deadline) is a near-copy; read the dates carefully.
g: Sources differ in summaries; this card follows the masterfile digest and the 2025 Reviewer, both of which state the petition was granted.
s: COMELEC cannot cut short registration that runs until 120 days before the election unless it proves necessity.

r: Excluding voters of highly urbanized cities (and of component cities whose charters so provide) from voting for provincial officials does not violate equal protection or impose a ‘substantive requirement’: the classification by income is reasonable, and there is no right to vote for officials of a unit that does not govern you. A prohibited ‘substantive requirement’ is a burden on suffrage that achieves no permissible State objective; here voters face no added condition. Income is a substantial distinction because it shows a city’s capacity to exist and develop independently, and independence from the province carries the loss of a vote in its elections.
f: Voters of Cebu City and Mandaue City challenged BP 51, which barred them from voting for Cebu provincial officials.
h: BP 51 upheld.
x: Use when a law changes which voters may vote for which offices (e.g., new provinces, HUC conversions). Under the 1987 Constitution, Art. X, Sec. 12 keeps the rule: voters of highly urbanized cities, and of component cities whose charters prohibit it, do not vote for provincial officials.

r: Absentee voting by Filipinos abroad (RA 9189) is an exception to the residence requirement under Art. V, Sec. 2; the affidavit of intent to return is valid. But a Joint Congressional Oversight Committee that reviews and approves COMELEC’s rules violates COMELEC’s independence, and COMELEC cannot canvass and proclaim the President and Vice President (Congress does). The affidavit is how an immigrant or permanent resident abroad shows that the Philippine domicile was never abandoned; by necessary implication, Art. V, Sec. 2 carves overseas voters out of the residence requirement of Sec. 1.
f: A lawyer challenged several provisions of the Overseas Absentee Voting Act of 2003.
h: Law upheld except the JCOC approval provisions and the COMELEC proclamation of President and Vice President.
x: Use with ABAKADA for legislative vetoes over independent bodies; also overseas voting questions. RA 9189 is now amended by RA 10590 (Overseas Voting Act of 2013).
s: Overseas absentee voting valid; a JCOC approving COMELEC rules violates its independence.

r: ‘Government’ in the sedition law means the system or institutions of government, not the persons who run it (the administration). Attacking officials’ character is not an attack on the government.
f: Editors were convicted of seditious libel for an editorial attacking the Civil Commission’s appointments of Filipinos.
h: Conviction reversed.
x: Distinguish ‘government’ from ‘administration’; useful when officials treat criticism as an attack on the State.

r: The National Centennial Commission chair holds a public office: the commission was created by law (executive issuance), exercised a sovereign function (promoting national culture and heritage), and served the public. The Ombudsman may investigate him even if he received no compensation. Governmental functions advance the public welfare and carry out sovereign duties under a State policy; proprietary functions serve only a local or special community benefit (e.g., a town fiesta) with no State policy involved. The temporary or honorary character of the post does not matter.
f: Salvador Laurel, NCC chair and CEO of Expocorp, was investigated for graft over Centennial Expo contracts.
h: Petition dismissed; the Ombudsman had jurisdiction.
x: What is a public office (Mechem’s elements); ‘governmental’ functions include promotion of culture.
test: Public office (Mechem, as applied in Laurel): (1) created by law; (2) delegated a portion of sovereign power; (3) has continuance, even if temporary; (4) powers and scope defined by law; (5) exercised for the public benefit.

n: Co Kim Cham v. Valdez Tan Keh
sub: IV.C De facto and de jure government
r: The Japanese-sponsored governments were de facto governments of paramount force; their judicial acts not of a political complexion remain valid after liberation (postliminy), and restored courts may continue pending cases without an enabling law. That the Philippine Executive Commission was a civil rather than a military body did not matter, since its authority came from the Japanese military. While it lasts, such a government must be obeyed in civil matters; under the Hague Regulations the occupant may suspend laws but must respect the municipal laws on public order and commerce. MacArthur’s proclamation voiding the ‘processes’ of other governments did not reach judicial processes.
f: A judge refused to continue a civil case begun during the Japanese occupation, citing MacArthur’s proclamation voiding the occupation government’s processes.
h: Mandamus granted; proceedings continue.
x: Kinds of de facto government (usurper, paramount force, secession) and the validity of their acts.

r: During the interregnum (Feb. 25, 1986 to the Freedom Constitution), there was no Constitution or Bill of Rights, but the revolutionary government remained bound by the ICCPR and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Seizures beyond the warrant were invalid. Its directives were the supreme law but valid only if (1) the enforcers did not exceed the authority the revolutionary government granted and (2) they did not violate the Covenant or the Declaration. EDSA was revolutionary because it was done in defiance of the 1973 Constitution after the Batasan proclaimed Marcos the winner.
f: A raid on the house of a general’s associate seized cash, jewelry and items not listed in the warrant, under a revolutionary government.
h: Items not in the warrant were ordered returned; the PCGG also lacked jurisdiction over persons not shown to be Marcos associates.
x: Use for ‘revolutionary government’ talk in the news: a sitting president elected under the Constitution cannot declare one without repudiating that Constitution.
g: Gatmaytan’s book quotes this case for Aquino’s government being ‘indisputably revolutionary’.
s: During the interregnum there was no Bill of Rights, but the revolutionary government was bound by the ICCPR and UDHR.

r: Parens patriae lets the State protect minors but supplements, not supplants, parents’ primary right. Curfew ordinances restricting minors’ fundamental rights are tested by strict scrutiny: compelling interest plus least restrictive means. Minors may be treated differently because of their peculiar vulnerability, their inability to make critical decisions in an informed and mature manner, and the importance of the parental role in child rearing.
f: Manila, Navotas and Quezon City adopted curfews for minors after Oplan Rody.
h: Manila and Navotas ordinances struck down as not narrowly drawn: their exceptions ignored minors’ exercise of free association, religion, assembly and expression at night. Manila’s fines and imprisonment on minors also conflict with the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act, which bars penalizing status offenses such as curfew violations; community service (Navotas) is a valid sanction. Quezon City ordinance upheld because its exceptions were narrowly drawn.
x: Any LGU regulation targeting minors or a vulnerable class; also a model of strict-scrutiny analysis. Parens patriae alone does not let the President order the detention of loitering minors; that needs a statute.
s: Parens patriae supplements parents; curfews on minors face strict scrutiny (least restrictive means).

r: A suit against an official is not a suit against the State if it seeks only to nullify an ultra vires act (no financial charge on the State), or if the official is sued personally for tortious acts beyond authority. Unauthorized acts of officials are not acts of the State. Had PASI sought damages on the nullity claims or impleaded the DOTC itself, the suit would have been one against the State (obiter).
f: A DOTC undersecretary offered for bidding an orbital slot already promised to PASI under an MOU, and allegedly defamed PASI’s CEO.
h: Immunity did not bar the injunction, nullity, and damages claims against the official.
x: Whenever an official raises state immunity, ask what relief is sought and whether it would charge the treasury.
test: Suit against an officer is a suit against the State if a judgment would require the State to act or pay. Exceptions: (1) the officer acted beyond authority or illegally; (2) the State has no interest in the outcome; (3) personal liability for tort.
s: Not a suit against the State if it only nullifies an ultra vires act or sues the official personally for torts.

r: A foreign agent acting within his official functions, with the host State’s consent to his activities, shares his State’s immunity (par in parem non habet imperium). Diplomatic immunity depends on performing diplomatic functions; a DEA attaché is not automatically a diplomat. Conferring diplomatic status is an executive prerogative. Consent was shown by official exchanges and the Philippine narcotics team’s presence at the arrest. A foreign agent sued in his personal capacity for acts beyond his functions, contrary to law and injurious to others, is not immune.
f: An Iranian national acquitted of drug charges sued a US DEA agent who had set up a buy-bust with Philippine narcotics officers.
h: Complaint dismissed: the agent was immune as an agent of the US acting with the Philippine government’s imprimatur.
x: Foreign officials sued in Philippine courts.
s: A foreign agent acting within official functions with host-State consent shares his State’s immunity.

r: An implementing agency of a foreign State must first be classified: if incorporated, its suability depends on its charter or the general law (‘sue and be sued’), regardless of its functions. Immunity must be properly established, e.g., by a DFA certification. GTZ was organized under German private law; absent proof of foreign law, processual presumption treats that law as the same as ours, so GTZ is like a corporation without an original charter that consents to suit under the Corporation Code. The Labor Arbiter therefore had jurisdiction.
f: Filipino employees of GTZ, the German implementing agency in a health insurance project, sued for illegal dismissal; GTZ claimed immunity.
h: GTZ failed to establish immunity: it did not show it was unincorporated or immune under its own law, and had no DFA certification of immunity. Its petition was denied.
x: Foreign state enterprises and incorporated agencies.

r: The State cannot invoke immunity to avoid paying for a public work it has accepted and used; justice demands payment on quantum meruit even if the contract is void for lack of formalities. The contractor’s failure to exhaust remedies before COA was excused because the issue was one of law and strict application would cause injustice; the contract was void for lack of appropriation and certification, but the State may not be unjustly enriched.
f: A contractor completed DPWH dike works in Pampanga; DPWH refused payment, invoking immunity and a void contract.
h: Payment on quantum meruit ordered (through COA).
x: Immunity cannot be an instrument of injustice; implied consent when the State benefits.

r: US Navy officers sued for the USS Guardian’s grounding on Tubbataha Reef are immune: a suit against them in their official capacity is a suit against the United States, and the writ of kalikasan cannot be used to collect damages or nullify the VFA. The flag State bears international responsibility under UNCLOS. Satisfying a judgment would require remedial action and appropriation of funds by the US, so the suit is against the US itself (par in parem non habet imperium).
f: Petitioners sought a writ of kalikasan against US officers and Philippine officials after a US minesweeper ran aground in Tubbataha in 2013.
h: Petition denied.
x: The 2013 midterm asked about this exact story (Colmenares). Foreign warship immunity, standing (Rules on Environmental Cases), and limits of kalikasan.
s: US warship officers immune for official acts; the flag State answers internationally; kalikasan cannot collect damages.

r: Government funds are not subject to garnishment or execution, even if an appropriation exists. Once liability is fixed by judgment, the claimant must file a money claim with COA, which has primary jurisdiction.
f: After DPWH failed to pay a compromise on just compensation for land taken for flood control, the RTC garnished DPWH funds.
h: Garnishment set aside; claim to be filed with COA, with legal interest.
x: Use when a court or claimant tries to seize public funds (consent to be sued is not consent to execution).
s: Public funds cannot be garnished; money claims go to COA.

n: Rubi v. Provincial Board of Mindoro
r: Police power, ‘the law of overruling necessity’, justified confining the Mangyans to a reservation; the classification by degree of civilization was upheld, and delegating to the provincial board the choice of site was valid (discretion in execution, not in making the law). The Court reasoned that the order was not a deprivation of liberty at all: segregation was ‘protection’ to make the Mangyans ‘useful citizens’, so habeas corpus could not issue.
f: Mangyans were ordered to live on a reservation under the Administrative Code; those who refused were detained.
h: Habeas corpus denied; law upheld (with a strong dissent on due process).
x: Historical police power case; read critically as a product of colonial policy. The DG reviewer flags it as possibly bad law: its premise that a cultural minority may be confined ‘for their own good’ clashes with equal protection and the 1987 Constitution’s recognition of indigenous cultural communities (Art. II, Sec. 22; Art. XII, Sec. 5). Cite it for the definition of police power, not for its result.

r: Requiring early warning devices on motor vehicles is a valid exercise of police power; it is reasonable and not confiscatory, and the delegation to the LTO to implement it had a sufficient standard. The Court also relied on the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Signs and Signals, which the Philippines signed and which recommends such safety devices, and on accident statistics showing the need.
f: A car owner challenged LOI 229 requiring early warning triangles as oppressive and an undue delegation.
h: LOI 229 and its rules upheld.
x: Classic police power and delegation case for safety regulations.

r: Closing Boracay for six months for rehabilitation was a valid police power measure (lawful subject: environment and health; lawful means: reasonably necessary, not unduly oppressive). The effect on travel was incidental; livelihood expectancies of informal workers must yield to the general welfare. The measure served compelling interests (a balanced and healthful ecology, and health), and six months was a reasonable period for major, permanent rehabilitation works that could not be done with tourists on the island. The majority also held that the President did not intrude on local autonomy.
f: Proclamation 475 declared a state of calamity and temporarily closed Boracay; a worker and a resident challenged it.
h: Petition dismissed; Proclamation 475 valid. Dissent: Proclamation 475 rests on RA 10121, whose state-of-calamity remedies (Sec. 17: price ceilings, monitoring of overpricing and hoarding, reprogramming of funds, no-interest loans) nowhere authorize the President or the NDRRMC to close an entire island. Police power is lodged in Congress, so the President may use it only under a valid delegation that passes the completeness and sufficient standard tests, and there was none. The dissent also said the President exercised control, not mere general supervision (Art. X, Sec. 4), over LGUs that RA 10121 tasks with disaster response.
x: A government closure or regulation burdening businesses and workers: apply the lawful subject and lawful means test. Argue both sides: lawful subject and lawful means (majority), but first ask whether any statute actually delegates the power to the executive (dissent).
s: Boracay closure is valid police power: lawful subject, lawful means; effects on travel incidental.

n: Iloilo I Electric Cooperative v. Executive Secretary
r: Public utility franchises cannot be exclusive and are subject to amendment or repeal by Congress for the common good (Art. XII, Sec. 11). Expanding MORE Power’s franchise into cooperatives’ areas (RA 11918) is valid; contract and franchise rights yield to police power. A franchise is a privilege, not the franchisee’s private property; as a grant it is beyond the non-impairment clause, and property rights bow to police power (Carlos Superdrug).
f: Three Iloilo electric cooperatives challenged a law extending MORE Electric and Power’s franchise into their coverage areas.
h: Petition dismissed (Zalameda, J.; Leonen, J., dissenting). Leonen, J. dissented: electricity distribution is a natural monopoly, so duplicate distributors raise costs against the public interest. Art. XII, Sec. 19 lets the State regulate monopolies when the public interest requires, and Sec. 11 allows amending a franchise only for the common good, so the expansion had to be justified by the common good, not by introducing competition alone.
x: Laws that impose new duties on regulated private businesses (franchises, utilities): non-impairment yields to police power; no exclusive franchise.
w: Do not confuse with PECO v. MORE (Iloilo City distribution assets), a different case.
s: Franchises are never exclusive and yield to the common good; non-impairment yields to police power.
